o: We must bring `1` to index 0 and `n` to index n-1 using adjacent swaps, minimizing swaps. Each adjacent swap moves an element one position, so moving `1` from position `i` to 0 costs `i` swaps and moving `n` from position `j` to n-1 costs `n-1-j` swaps. In Example 2 (`[2,4,1,3]`), 1 is at index 2 (cost 2) and 3=n is at index 3 (cost 0), yet the answer is 3, not 2 — because when 1 passes n's original position they 'cross', saving nothing but requiring care: if 1 starts right of n, one swap moves both toward their targets simultaneously, so subtract 1. With n ≤ 50, even full simulation works, but the closed form is trivial.
k: Each swap shifts one element by one slot, so cost equals distance traveled.
If 1's index is greater than n's index, their paths overlap and one swap serves both, so subtract 1.

a.i: Locate 1 and n. The answer is the sum of their distances to the ends, minus 1 if 1 currently sits to the right of n (they share one swap while crossing).
s: Find i = index of 1 and j = index of n.
Answer = i + (n-1-j), minus 1 if i > j.
a.t: O(n) — one scan to find both indices

w: The formula solution is ideal; a brute-force simulation (repeatedly bubbling 1 left and n right) also passes given n ≤ 50 but is unnecessary. Pitfall: forgetting the −1 correction when 1 starts right of n. Verify with `[2,4,1,3]` (answer 3) and already-sorted inputs (answer 0).
